The Problem

0:00 to 0:27 · 67 words

Good afternoon. We are Team Kairos, and this is the problem we built for.

A message lands on WhatsApp. Someone's sister needs surgery, an account number attached. Most of us scroll past. Not because we do not care, but because we cannot check.

It costs nothing to fake. And even with real NGOs, donors give into a pool and are never told what their own money achieved.

Next 2 · The Solutionpress →
2 / 6

The Solution

0:27 to 0:57 · 75 words

Kairos is the trusted middle layer. Three steps.

The cause is checked before it raises anything. Identity verified, and an AI interviewer turns the story and the evidence into a published, itemised budget.

The money is held against that budget. It can only ever be paid to a named, verified counterparty, never to the organiser.

And the moment a payment goes out, every donor is told their exact share of it, with the invoice attached.

Who It Is For

0:57 to 1:18 · 53 words

Nigerians already give constantly, but to people they know. Every WhatsApp appeal with an account number is our market, and there are thousands every week.

We enter at school fees, because there the rail verifies for us. A Remita reference belongs to one student, one fee, one school account, and cannot be redirected.

74 questions
▸How do you actually pay a school?prepared

For a federal institution the student generates a Remita reference on the school portal. It is tied to one student, one fee and one school account, and anyone holding it can pay it. We confirm it is the school and that the amount is right, we pay it, and the receipt is automatic. For a private school it is their payment link, or an invoice to an account we have confirmed belongs to them.

▸What stops the organiser inflating the invoice?prepared

Three things. The AI compares budget lines against normal prices and flags an outlier before the cause goes live. The money goes to the hospital's own verified account against the hospital's own invoice, so inflating it now needs the hospital's finance department to be in on it. And the ledger is public, so anyone can inspect the price.

▸What about a market caterer with no CAC registration?prepared

We do not claim we can verify them as a business, and I would not trust anyone who told you they had solved that. We verify the person behind the account with their BVN, we check they are not connected to the organiser, we cap how much can go to them, and we release the rest only after proof of delivery. The fraud we cannot prevent is small, traceable to a real identity, and visible to everyone.

▸How will you make money?prepared

We are not trying to. We take two percent of a donation, capped at five thousand naira for the whole cause, which covers what that cause costs us to run. Anything above that goes into a public pool that makes other causes free. The rest comes from grants, donated cloud and AI credits, and non-profit rates from payment providers.

▸Why should we believe it works, when it is a prototype?prepared

Because we built the half you cannot buy. The accounting is real: balances held against each budget line, per-donor attribution, trust levels and the public ledger are running code, and the rules that stop a payout are enforced on the server.

What is not real is the money movement. The identity check, the vendor check and the payments are simulated, no real naira has moved, and we have not signed the licensed partner who would hold the funds. Each of those will be an integration with a service that already exists. We keep the books as though the money moved; what is stubbed is the moving.

▸You say escrow accounting is real. Are you holding people's money right now?prepared

No, and the phrasing deserves the challenge. Escrow accounting means we keep the books: every naira is tracked against a budget line, each donor's share of every payment is computed, and the ledger is generated from that. All of that is running code.

What we are not doing is holding funds. No real money has entered the system, the payments are simulated, and the licensed partner who would hold escrow is not signed. We account for it as though it moved. It has not.

▸How do you verify a Remita RRR?prepared

The organiser puts the twelve digit reference on the budget line instead of an account number. Before any money moves we ask Remita's system what that reference is for. It tells us which school it belongs to, how much it is for, and whether it has already been paid. We compare all three against the published budget line, and the payment is blocked if any of them disagree.

We never ask for the school's account number, because that reference can only ever reach the school. It cannot be redirected to anyone. And the proof is automatic: after we pay, we check the reference again, it now reads paid, and that receipt goes straight onto the public ledger and into every donor's message.

Remita built that lookup, not us. We are not a rival to them. We are just another customer paying a bill through their system, the same way a parent would. Everywhere else in Kairos we have to check a supplier ourselves. Here we do not have to, and that is why we are starting with school fees.

▸How do you verify BVN or NIN? How does the system know it is legit?prepared

The check is not ours to make, and that is the point. You cannot query NIMC or NIBSS directly. We call a licensed verification partner, send the number and the name, and they return the record the government holds, including the registered name and the photograph on file.

The number on its own proves nothing, because numbers leak and can be bought. The verification is the comparison. The name has to match the record, and above a threshold we ask for a selfie, check that it is a live person rather than a photograph, and match it against the picture the registry returns. That is the step that proves the person is who they claim, rather than that they know somebody's number. Legitimacy comes from the licence and the face match, not from anything clever we wrote.

Three things we commit to around it. We store a token and the result, never the number itself. We show the partner's name on screen at the moment we ask, so you know where your data is going. And we ask only the organiser, only at the moment they publish and start asking strangers for money. Donors never verify. The patient or the student never verifies.

▸What is crowdfunding, and what do you mean by moving proof?prepared

Crowdfunding is raising small amounts from many people for one thing. Here it usually means an account number in a WhatsApp group. On those, the money is collected and sent to the person who asked, and that is where it ends. On Kairos the money never reaches that person. It can only be paid to the hospital or the school on the budget, and when it moves, each donor is told what their own share paid for. Both move money. Only one can show you where it landed.

▸What stops someone taking a patient's bill from a hospital and raising money off it?prepared

They can steal the story. They cannot steal the destination. The money can only go to the hospital named on that bill, into an account we have confirmed belongs to that hospital. So if they raise two million on a real bill, the two million pays that real bill. To get it themselves they would need an account that passes a company check and a name match against a teaching hospital, and their own account will not. Add a verified identity on the attempt, a flag if the bill has been used before, and a small cap for first-timers. What we do not fully solve is consent: someone could fund a stranger's real bill without asking them. The fix is confirming with the patient or the hospital before we release, and we should build it.

▸What stops you, the people running Kairos, from stealing the money?prepared

Three things, and the first is the one that matters. The money never sits in a Kairos account. It sits with a licensed partner, separate from our own money. We instruct, they move it. Second, a payment can only reach an account already verified and attached to a published budget line. There is no screen anywhere, including for us, that lets anyone type a fresh account number and send money to it. Third, every naira in and out is on a public page, so a theft is not a hidden entry in a back office, it is a visible hole that the donors are looking at. We do not claim to have solved insider fraud. We have made sure we never hold the cash and cannot move it anywhere that is not already public.

▸How do you know the school fees were actually paid, and what if someone else pays the reference first?prepared

We do not generate the reference, the student does on the school portal, so we are only ever paying something that already exists. After we pay we look it up again, and the school's own system confirms it is settled and issues the receipt. The proof comes from them, not from us. And we check before we pay too. If it already reads paid, we stop and the money stays put. If it is settled while we are paying, the reference can only be settled once, so our payment just fails. Then that budget line is closed and the money either moves to another line, with donors told, or goes back to them in proportion. If a relative quietly paid first, that is a good outcome, and the donors get their money back.

▸What does two percent capped at five thousand naira mean?prepared

For every thousand naira donated we take twenty. We stop once we have taken five thousand from that cause in total, not per donation, for the whole cause. So a two hundred and fifty thousand naira cause pays five thousand, and so does a twenty million naira one. Checking a cause costs the same either way, so the cap means we cannot profit from a big cause even if we wanted to. It is not a promise to behave, it is a limit that makes the promise unnecessary.

▸Aren't there other giving platforms in Nigeria already?prepared

Yes, and two kinds. The school fee companies, Edusko, Schoolable, Edubanc, are lenders. The parent repays with interest. That is debt, ours is a gift. The donation platforms collect money and send it to the fundraiser's account, where it becomes invisible again. Their job is to help you raise. Ours is to show you what the raise did. Everyone else answers "did the money get raised?" We are the only ones answering "did the money do what it said?" And honestly the competitor is not another app, it is the WhatsApp account number, which costs nothing and promises nothing.

▸Who pays the people running Kairos?prepared

Straight answer: the two percent does not, and was never meant to. It covers what a cause costs to process. At the start nobody is paid from it. We build it part-time, funded by grants, prizes and donated cloud and AI credits. To make it somebody's full-time job there are three realistic routes, and none is the donation fee: grant funding, which exists precisely to pay salaries for this kind of work; partner organisations sponsoring the running costs of a batch of causes; and companies matching staff giving on a flat licence. If none of those come through, this stays a side project that works rather than becoming a job. We would rather say that than pretend a capped two percent turns into salaries.

▸How will you get people to use it?prepared

Not by waiting for strangers. We go to groups that already hold people together, a church with a student welfare fund, an alumni group that already does this informally every session, a small NGO with a mailing list. They arrive with their own donors who already trust them, so nobody has to trust Kairos on day one. We are borrowing trust that exists and giving them a better way to run what they already do. School fees suit this because the need arrives on a timetable and the school confirms payment within minutes. The first twenty causes matter more than the next two thousand, because each one that finishes with receipts is the only marketing a trust product really has.

▸Shouldn't verification be strict enough to scare off dishonest people?prepared

Hard to fake and hard to do are not the same thing, and most platforms confuse them. More documents does not mean harder to deceive, it mostly annoys honest people. So: only the person asking for money verifies, never the donor and never the patient. We ask at publish rather than at sign-up, and say why on screen. And the strictness follows the money, so a fifty thousand naira cause needs an ID that matches a name, while a five million naira one needs a face match, supplier checks and staged release. The friction is not evenly felt. The honest person does one check once. The dishonest one hits a wall at every stage, because he is the one who cannot pass a face match or make a bank account name match a hospital's.

▸If someone shares a cause, is it just a link? I wouldn't open a random link.prepared

You are right, and a bare link would kill it. When a Kairos link is pasted into WhatsApp, the cause's preview card appears under it: title, picture, how much is raised, the goal, and how many people have given, all before anyone taps. That is already built. What is missing is the sentence in front, because the share button currently copies the address and nothing else. It should copy a short editable message with it, naming the person, the amount and the hospital. Small to build, and it is the difference between a link people open and one they ignore.

▸Who is on the team?prepared

Four of us. Name them here, with one phrase each on what they do.

▸What happens if a cause does not reach its goal?anticipated

Nothing is paid out that cannot be paid in full. Escrow holds the money against named budget lines, so a half-funded surgery does not become a half-paid hospital. The organiser can narrow the budget to what has been raised, with donors told what changed, or the money goes back to donors in proportion to what they gave. Our fee goes back with it.

▸What if the organiser disappears halfway through?anticipated

The money does not go anywhere, because it was never theirs to move. It sits in escrow against the remaining budget lines. Anything unspent is refunded pro-rata. Walking away costs them their verified identity on the platform and costs the donors nothing.

▸Can a donor get a refund?anticipated

Yes, in two cases. If the cause does not deliver and escrow is returned, and if a budget line is cancelled or settled by someone else. What a donor cannot do is pull back money already paid to a hospital, because at that point it is the hospital's money and the receipt is on the ledger. We would rather be clear about that than imply a guarantee we cannot honour.

▸What stops a hospital inflating its price because it knows a donor is paying?anticipated

Three things. The AI screens budget lines against normal prices for that procedure at intake, so an outlier is flagged before the cause goes live. The invoice is the hospital's own, issued in their system, not a number the organiser typed. And the price is public, inspectable by anyone including other hospitals. It does not make overcharging impossible, it makes it arguable in public.

▸What if a cause raises more than it needs?anticipated

The raise stops at the goal. If extra arrives first, the organiser can add a budget line, which donors are told about, or the surplus is returned in proportion. What we will not do is quietly roll it into a different cause, because the donor gave to this one.

▸Why would a hospital or school agree to be paid this way?anticipated

They do not have to agree to anything new. We pay an invoice or a reference they already issued, into the account they already use, through the same channels anyone else would use. From their side, a third party settled a bill. That is the point of paying an obligation rather than a person: it needs no cooperation to work.

▸What if the AI approves a cause it should not have?anticipated

It will, eventually. That is why it is not the only control. Anything the checks flag stops and waits for a person. A new organiser can only raise a small amount. Money still cannot leave escrow except toward a verified counterparty on a published budget. And the ledger is public from the first naira. The AI is the first filter, not the last, and the damage a mistake can do is capped by everything behind it.

▸Is this legal? Do you need a licence to hold donations?anticipated

We do not hold the money, which is the part that matters. Escrow sits with a licensed partner in an account separate from ours. Alongside that we register as a non-profit with trustees under CAC, register with SCUML because we handle donations at scale, register with the NDPC for the identity data, and publish an annual account of what came in and what it cost to run.

▸What stops two people raising for the same hospital bill?anticipated

The invoice. A budget line points at a specific invoice or reference, and once it is settled it reads as paid in the hospital's or school's own system. The second cause pointing at it gets blocked at the check we run before paying, and that money is returned. Duplicate stories are possible. Duplicate payments are not.

▸Can people give anonymously?anticipated

Yes, and the app already supports it. Your name can be hidden from the public page while the attribution still works, so you receive your own receipts and the ledger still balances. Anonymous to the crowd, never anonymous to the accounting.

▸Who earns the interest on money sitting in escrow?anticipated

Not us. Money held in escrow belongs to the causes. Float is one of the quiet ways payment businesses actually make money, and taking it would contradict the entire product. If we ever wanted it, we would have to ask for it in public.

▸What is your single biggest risk?anticipated

Distribution, not fraud. The controls are the part we have thought hardest about. Getting the first twenty causes onto the platform, from organisations that already have donors, is what decides whether this exists in a year. It is also why we start with school fees, where the need arrives on a timetable and the proof is instant.

▸Why has nobody done this already?anticipated

Pieces of it exist. Watsi pays hospitals directly, GoFundMe does scale, Remita does references, the lenders do school fees. What nobody has done is put escrow, pay-the-provider and a per-donor receipt together in a market where trust is the actual bottleneck. It is not technically hard. It is unglamorous, and it only makes sense if you accept you are building a trust layer rather than a payments business.

▸Who exactly is the user?anticipated

Two people. The organiser, an ordinary person with a real need and no track record, and the donor, who wants to help but cannot tell a real appeal from a fake one. Both are already doing this on WhatsApp today, badly. We are not creating a behaviour, we are giving one that already exists somewhere safe to happen.

▸How do you actually check a Remita RRR, step by step?technical

Four steps, and we only ever touch a reference somebody else created.

One. The student generates the reference on their school portal. We do not generate it and we could not. It is twelve digits, issued by the institution's own system, and it already carries a student, a fee and the school's settlement account.

Two. The organiser types it on the budget line where a bank account would normally go. Nobody types an account number anywhere.

Three. Before any money moves we call Remita's status lookup for that reference. It returns who the biller is, what the amount is, and whether it has already been paid. We compare all three against the published budget line. Wrong school, wrong amount, or already settled, and the payment is blocked and the money stays in escrow.

Four. We pay the reference through a bill-payment channel, then call the same lookup again. It now reads paid and a receipt exists. That receipt, from the school's system and not from us, is what goes on the public ledger and into every donor's message.

The practical detail is that the lookup needs a merchant account with Remita and the request is signed with a hash of your API key, so this is a contract to sign rather than a problem to solve. It is not built in the prototype yet, and it is the next thing we build.

▸How do you actually check a BVN or NIN?technical

You cannot call NIMC or NIBSS directly, so you do not. You sign with a licensed verification partner, Prembly, Dojah, Youverify, Smile ID or similar, and they hold the licence.

You send the number and the name. They return the record the government holds: registered name, date of birth, and usually the photograph on file.

The number alone proves nothing, because numbers leak and are openly sold. The check is the comparison. The typed name has to match the registry name, and above a threshold we also take a selfie, confirm it is a live person rather than a photo, and match it against the registry picture. That is what proves the person is who they claim rather than that they know someone's number.

For NIN the clean path is the virtual NIN, a short-lived token the user generates with *346*3#, so we verify a token and never handle the eleven digits at all.

▸How do you check that a bank account really belongs to the hospital?technical

One API call, and it is the cheapest and most important check in the whole product.

It is called a name enquiry. You send a bank code and an account number, and NIBSS returns the name on that account. Your payment processor already exposes it; on Paystack it is the bank resolve endpoint.

Then you compare three names: the one on the CAC company record, the one the name enquiry returned, and the one written on the budget line. They have to agree, allowing for ordinary spelling differences.

That is what stops money labelled LUTH landing in a personal account. It is instant, close to free, and it is the single check that does the most work.

▸How do you check that a company exists?technical

A CAC lookup by RC number through the same verification partner. It returns the registered name, the status, and the registration date.

On its own it proves very little, because anyone can register a company. It matters because of what it feeds: the registered name is what the account name has to match. We also check a tax identification number where there is one, and for hospitals the state accreditation body, which in Lagos is HEFAMAA.

The useful way to think about it is that we are not verifying an entity, we are verifying a triple: the entity, the account, and the invoice. Any one alone is weak. Together they close the loop.

▸How is my share of a payment calculated?technical

Plain arithmetic, and the code does it the moment money moves.

Take the payment as a fraction of everything the cause has raised. If a cause raised one million naira and a seven hundred thousand naira payment goes out, that payment is seventy percent of the pot.

Apply that same fraction to your own gift. You gave seven thousand, so seventy percent of your gift, four thousand nine hundred naira, went to that hospital.

Every donor gets that calculation at the same instant, which is why nobody writes those messages. It is one line of maths run across everyone who gave.

▸Does it add up exactly, to the last naira?technical

Not quite, and it is worth saying so.

Each donor's share is rounded to the nearest naira. Across eighty donors those roundings can leave the shares adding up to a few naira more or less than the payment itself.

The payment and the ledger are exact. It is only the per-donor slices that round. The fix is to give the remainder to the largest donor, or carry it to the next disbursement, and that needs doing before real money moves.

▸What stops the same money being spent twice out of escrow?technical

Five checks run on the server before any payment is recorded, and all five have to pass.

You have to be the organiser of that cause. The vendor on that budget line has to be verified. The amount has to be more than zero. It cannot exceed what is left in escrow. And it cannot exceed what is left unspent on that specific budget line.

That last one is the one people miss. Escrow is not one pot you can drain, it is divided across the published budget, and each line can only ever pay out what it was promised.

▸What if the payment goes out but your server crashes halfway?technical

Today, nothing protects you, and I would rather say that than bluff. A retried request could record a payment twice.

Two things fix it and neither is exotic. An idempotency key, so the same payment instruction submitted twice is recognised and applied once. And a database transaction around the whole operation, so the payment record, the escrow balance and the donor notifications all commit together or none of them do. MongoDB supports it, we have not wired it.

It does not matter in a prototype where no real money moves. It is non-negotiable before any does.

▸Could someone just edit the ledger in the database?technical

Today, someone with database access could, and any honest answer has to start there.

That is exactly why the production design does not keep the money with us. Escrow sits with a licensed partner, and their records are not ours to edit. The ledger we publish is reconciled against theirs.

A ledger you can edit is not evidence. A ledger that has to match the bank's is.

▸How would you actually detect a reused photo?technical

Not by comparing files, because changing one pixel defeats that. You store a perceptual fingerprint of every image, a short code derived from what the picture looks like rather than its bytes, so a cropped, resized or recompressed copy still fingerprints close to the original. A new upload gets compared against every fingerprint already on the platform.

Alongside that, photographs carry hidden data: when they were taken and often where. If the story says last month and the photo says two years ago in another state, that is a flag.

In the prototype these results are hardcoded to pass. The mechanism is standard, it is just not wired yet.

▸What is it built with?technical

Next.js with the App Router, MongoDB through Mongoose, TypeScript, Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. The interface is deliberately Twitter-shaped so nobody has to learn it.

The intake interviewer is Claude Haiku, called with a schema so the conversation comes back as structured fields rather than prose, and it falls back to a scripted interviewer if the model is unreachable.

Nothing here is exotic, on purpose. The hard part of this product is the money logic and the verification, not the framework.

▸How does the AI interviewer actually work?technical

It is a real model call, not a decision tree. The model is given the role of a careful intake officer and the conversation is constrained by a schema, so whatever it asks, what comes back is always the same shape: a title, a story, an itemised budget with named vendors, a list of evidence, and a set of screening findings.

That is why it can ask different follow-up questions every time and still produce something the database can store. It asks like a person and returns like a form.

At the end it reports three to five findings on what it just heard: whether the dates hang together, whether vendors were actually named, whether the budget is proportionate. Those are judgements about the conversation, not checks against an external record, and we should not describe them as verification.

▸What stops someone calling your API directly instead of using the app?technical

Nothing stops them calling it, and nothing needs to. Every rule lives on the server, not in the browser.

The check that you are the organiser, the check that the vendor is verified, the check against the escrow balance and against the remaining budget line, the raise limit for your trust level, all of it runs server-side on every request, from your session rather than from anything the client sends.

A hand-made request is just a request. It meets the same five checks, and fails them the same way.

▸How do GoFundMe and the others verify people?competitors

Strictly, but only in one direction. Before anyone can withdraw, they check legal name, address, date of birth, a government photo ID and a tax number, and the bank account receiving the money has to match the verified person. That is not generosity on their part, it is their payment processor obeying know-your-customer law.

So they can tell you exactly who withdrew the money. That is the half they do well, and we do the same thing with BVN or NIN.

▸Do they check that the story is true?competitors

Generally no, and they do not claim to. For ordinary campaigns nobody calls the hospital, asks for the bill, or confirms the patient exists before it goes live. They run on innocent until flagged.

What they do have is reactive: algorithms watching for stolen photos and copied text, a Report button for the public, and human investigators who demand hard proof once a campaign is flagged enough times. For big public disasters they will verify proactively, but that is the exception.

We do that checking at intake instead, before a naira is raised, because in a low-trust market the flag comes too late.

▸Do they verify that the money was spent on what was promised?competitors

No. Not one of them, and this is the gap the whole product sits in.

Once the funds are released to the organiser's bank account, the platform has no visibility and no control. No receipts, no proof of delivery, no check that the hospital was ever paid. Their own terms say they cannot guarantee funds are used as described, because the money has simply become the organiser's money.

They answer: is this a real person? We answer: did the money do what it said? Those are different questions and only one of them is what a donor actually worries about.

▸If they already do identity checks, what are you adding?competitors

Identity tells you who to blame afterwards. It does not stop anything happening.

A verified person can still raise two million naira on a true story, withdraw it, and spend it on something else, and every major platform would process that without a single alert. We added the part that comes after the check: the money never reaches them, it pays the hospital directly, and every donor gets the receipt.

Their verification is about recovery. Ours is about prevention.

▸Isn't community reporting enough?competitors

It works where there is a community watching. It fails exactly where we are.

Reporting is retrospective, so the money is usually gone by the time enough people click. It needs scale, and a new cause with forty donors does not have it. And it punishes the visible, so a loud fraud gets caught while a quiet one succeeds.

We would rather not need a crowd to notice. The budget is published before the raise, and the payment can only go to the counterparty named on it.

▸Why wouldn't GoFundMe just build this?competitors

They could build the software in a quarter. What they would have to give up is the model.

Paying providers instead of people means verifying a counterparty in every market they operate in, holding funds in escrow with the licensing that implies, and telling organisers they can no longer spend freely. That is slower, more expensive and less popular, and it would be a downgrade for the ninety percent of their users who are honest and in a high-trust market.

It is the right trade here and the wrong trade there. That is usually what a real opening looks like.

▸How realistic is it to actually get money back, on their platforms and on yours?competitors

On theirs, hard. Kickstarter does not refund at all, the creator is obliged to and your real recourse is suing them. GoFundMe runs a goodwill guarantee that is capped per donor and time-limited, funded out of their own pocket rather than a legal right. Card chargebacks only work inside a short window and by then the cash is usually spent.

On ours it is structurally easier, because the money has not moved. Anything still in escrow is returned in full and in proportion, immediately, and our charge goes back with it. That covers a cause that stalls, a goal that is missed, or a budget line someone else settles first.

What we cannot claw back is a payment already made to a hospital, because at that point it is theirs. That is a narrower promise than guaranteeing refunds, and it is one we can actually keep.

▸So what is the honest one-line difference?competitors

They verify the person. We verify the payment.

Everything else follows from that. They can tell a donor who took the money. We can show a donor what their own naira bought, with the receipt, the same day it happened.

▸The judge said you cannot just hold people's money. Is that right?escrow & law

Completely right, and it is the reason the architecture looks the way it does. We never hold it.

In Nigeria the licence most fintechs hold, a Payment Solution Service Provider licence, explicitly forbids holding customer funds. Only a Mobile Money Operator may hold them, and that needs capital we are nowhere near. So building our own wallet was never on the table.

What we do instead is instruct. Funds sit with a licensed partner in an account we do not control, and Kairos sends the instruction to pay a verified counterparty. The partner moves the money. We move the proof.

▸Isn't this the same as Ajo or esusu?escrow & law

No, and the difference is the one the regulator cares about. Ajo is a deposit. You pay in expecting your own money back, in your turn. That creates a liability to the contributor, which is why it attracts banking rules.

A donation is the opposite. It is given irrevocably to one named cause, with no promise of return, no interest and no yield. We do not pool across causes, so there is no float to lend out and nothing to roll over.

The only time money goes back is failure, when a cause does not deliver and the escrow is refunded. That is a refund, not a withdrawal.

▸Who actually holds the money then?escrow & law

One of three routes, and they are not exclusive.

An escrow-as-a-service provider. Pandascrow is the established Nigerian one, built exactly for this: milestone releases, an API, and the licence sits with them. Fincra and similar infrastructure players offer the same shape.

Or a bank or microfinance bank partnership. Each cause gets a dedicated virtual account, collections settle into a designated trust account the bank controls, and we instruct payouts. Providus, Safe Haven, VFD and Sterling all run this model for marketplaces.

And underneath both, the donations themselves are held on trust by a registered non-profit. Note Paystack does not do escrow, so our card checkout and our custody are deliberately two different partners.

▸What licences and registrations do you actually need?escrow & law

Four, and none of them is a banking licence.

CAC Part F, Incorporated Trustees, which is the legal form for a non-profit and the thing that lets donations be held on trust. SCUML with the EFCC, which is mandatory for non-profits because we are a designated non-financial institution; without it a bank will place a Post No Debit on the account. Registration with the NDPC, because we handle BVN or NIN data and medical evidence. And a contract with whoever holds the funds, who carries the CBN licence on our behalf.

What we deliberately do not need is a Mobile Money Operator licence, and we do not need it precisely because we never touch the money.

▸Could you not just make money on the float?escrow & law

We could, and a lot of payment businesses quietly do. It is incompatible with the product.

Interest earned on money held in escrow belongs to the causes, not to us, and we have put that in writing. A platform whose entire claim is that you can see where your money went cannot have a line of income the giver never sees.

It is also moot in practice: we do not hold the funds, the licensed partner does, so the float is not ours to take even if we wanted it.

▸Walk me through escrow end to end. Where does a naira physically sit?escrow & law

Four stops, and we only ever control the instruction, never the money.

One. The donor pays by card or transfer through a collection provider, Paystack or Flutterwave. That is checkout only. The money does not land with us.

Two. It settles into a designated account that a licensed partner controls, ring-fenced to that one cause. Either an escrow provider like Pandascrow, PayScrow or EscrowPay, or a bank or microfinance bank holding it in a trust account. Our name is not on it.

Three. It sits there against the published budget. Every line has a named counterparty and an amount, and the sum of the lines is the ceiling.

Four. The organiser instructs a payout. We run the checks, and if they pass we send the instruction to the partner. They move the money to the hospital, the school or the supplier. The receipt comes back and lands on the public ledger and in every donor's notification.

▸Is there such a thing as an escrow licence in Nigeria?escrow & law

No, and that surprises people. The CBN does not issue an escrow licence as a category. Escrow providers operate under the payment service provider framework, or they sit on a bank's trust-account infrastructure.

That is precisely why the question of who holds the money matters more than what anyone calls themselves. We are not looking for an escrow licence. We are contracting with a party that already has permission to hold funds, and we keep our own hands off it.

▸Why do you still name Paystack and Flutterwave if they do not do escrow?escrow & law

Because they do the other two jobs, and we should be precise about which is which.

Collection: taking a card or transfer from the donor at checkout. Payout: pushing money to a verified counterparty's account. Both are theirs. Custody, holding the money in between, is not, and Paystack does not offer it.

So the stack is three parties, not one. A collection provider at the front, a licensed partner holding escrow in the middle, and a payout rail at the back. The deck now says exactly that.

▸What stops the escrow partner itself from failing or freezing the funds?escrow & law

Nothing we can promise away, and it is the risk we inherit by not holding the money ourselves. What we can do is choose a partner that is regulated, keep the funds in a designated account rather than the partner's working capital, and reconcile our ledger against their statement so a discrepancy shows up as a gap rather than a silence.

It is a real exposure. It is still smaller than the alternative, which is a two-person team holding other people's donations in its own bank account.

▸How does escrow work when a cause has several budget lines?escrow & law

Escrow is not one pot. It is divided across the published budget, and each line can only ever pay out what it was promised.

So a cause holding four hundred thousand naira with a three hundred thousand surgery line and a hundred thousand medication line cannot put three fifty into the surgery. The check runs on both the overall balance and the remaining amount on that specific line. That is what makes the published budget a promise rather than a suggestion.

▸What happens to the money if Kairos shuts down?escrow & law

Because the funds sit with a licensed partner in a designated account and are ring-fenced per cause against a published budget, they do not form part of anything Kairos owns. If we disappear tomorrow, the undisbursed balance is still attributable to named causes and named donors, and it is refundable.

That is the practical case for not holding it ourselves. A startup failing should never be the reason a surgery goes unpaid.

▸You said AI checks the account before payout. Is that really AI, or just an API call?from the pitch

Both, and the split matters. Fetching the account name from the bank is an API call, not intelligence. What the model does is the comparison: is 'LUTH' the same entity as 'Lagos University Teaching Hospital', is 'Iya Basira Catering Svcs' the same as the name on the budget line, is this difference a spelling variant or a different business.

That is a judgement call on messy Nigerian naming, and it is where a model beats a string match. We would not call the lookup AI, and we should not.

▸You said the AI never decides who gets paid. Then what happens when it flags something?from the pitch

It stops the cause and waits for a person. A flag is not a rejection, it is a hold.

That matters because the model will be wrong in both directions. It will flag an honest person whose bill is dated oddly, and it will miss a careful liar. A hold costs the honest person a day. An automatic rejection would cost them the cause, and an automatic approval would cost the donors.

▸You start with school fees. What is your actual first cause, and who brings it?from the pitch

A student welfare group, a church fund, or an alumni set that already does this informally every session. They arrive with a real student, a real Remita reference, and a list of people who already give to them.

We are not asking strangers to trust Kairos on day one. We are asking a group that already collects money by WhatsApp to collect it somewhere it can be proven instead.

▸The receipt says seventy percent of a gift. What if I gave after that payment went out?from the pitch

Then that payment is not yours and you are not billed for it. Attribution runs over the donations that existed when the money moved, so a later donor is simply not in that slice.

Your money attaches to the next payment out, at whatever proportion the pot is then. Nobody is credited with a payment they did not fund.

▸You keep saying the money cannot reach the organiser. Can they not just name themselves as the vendor?from the pitch

They can try, and it is the first thing a fraudster tries. The account-name check kills it: a personal account will not match a registered business name, and we compare the payout account against the entity on the budget line before anything moves.

For an informal supplier where no company exists, the independence check does the same job from the other side. Shared BVN, phone, device or address between organiser and vendor blocks the payout automatically.

▸Your demo is seeded data. What happens the first time a real cause goes through?from the pitch

The money logic is the same code either way, so escrow, attribution and the ledger behave identically. What changes is that three stubs become real calls: identity to a licensed partner, the vendor check to a CAC and name-enquiry lookup, and payments to a collection provider.

The honest risk is not the arithmetic, it is the first real counterparty failing a check we have never run in anger. That is why the first causes are school fees, where the reference does the verifying for us.

▸What is the one thing most likely to go wrong in your first year?from the pitch

A real cause that passes every check and still does not deliver. Not fraud, just life: the patient is transferred, the supplier disappoints, the student withdraws.

Our controls make that visible and refundable rather than preventable, and we should not pretend otherwise. The money is still in escrow, so the donors get it back. What we lose is the thing we are actually selling, which is a completed story.

▸Why should a donor pay your fee when WhatsApp is free?from the pitch

They should not, if they already know and trust the person asking. Kairos is not for your sister's surgery, it is for a stranger's.

The fee buys the thing WhatsApp cannot give: the money cannot be diverted, and you get a receipt for your own share. Tentatively two percent capped at five thousand naira, visible before you confirm, and you can cover it so the cause still receives the full gift.

▸You have no users. Why is this not just a hackathon project?from the pitch

Right now that is a fair description, and the honest answer is that we have built the part that is hard to build and not yet the part that is hard to earn.

What makes it more than a demo is that the money logic is real and the sequencing is deliberate. We start with school fees because the rail verifies for us, we start with groups that already have donors, and we have written down which of our controls is weakest. That is a plan, not a prototype.

Nothing matches that.
